claim: Protein translocation across cell membranes is a ubiquitous process required for protein secretion and membrane protein insertion.
source: Protein translocation across cell membranes is a ubiquitous process required for protein secretion and membrane protein insertion.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the fundamental role of protein translocation.

claim: In bacteria, protein translocation is mostly mediated by the conserved SecYEG complex.
source: In bacteria, this is mostly mediated by the conserved SecYEG complex, driven through rounds of ATP hydrolysis by the cytoplasmic SecA, and the trans-membrane proton motive force.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the bacterial protein translocation machinery.

claim: Bacterial protein translocation is driven through rounds of ATP hydrolysis by the cytoplasmic SecA.
source: In bacteria, this is mostly mediated by the conserved SecYEG complex, driven through rounds of ATP hydrolysis by the cytoplasmic SecA, and the trans-membrane proton motive force.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the energy source for bacterial protein translocation.

claim: Bacterial protein translocation is driven by the trans-membrane proton motive force.
source: In bacteria, this is mostly mediated by the conserved SecYEG complex, driven through rounds of ATP hydrolysis by the cytoplasmic SecA, and the trans-membrane proton motive force.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the energy source for bacterial protein translocation.

claim: SecA has important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
source: The results show that SecA, both the signal sequence and mature components of the pre-protein, and ATP hydrolysis each have important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The signal sequence has important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
source: The results show that SecA, both the signal sequence and mature components of the pre-protein, and ATP hydrolysis each have important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mature components of the pre-protein have important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
source: The results show that SecA, both the signal sequence and mature components of the pre-protein, and ATP hydrolysis each have important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: ATP hydrolysis has important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
source: The results show that SecA, both the signal sequence and mature components of the pre-protein, and ATP hydrolysis each have important and specific roles in channel unlocking, opening and priming for transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: After channel opening, translocation proceeds in two phases: a slow phase independent of substrate length, and a length-dependent transport phase.
source: After channel opening, translocation proceeds in two phases: a slow phase independent of substrate length, and a length-dependent transport phase with an intrinsic translocation rate of ~40 amino acids per second for the proOmpA substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing dwell time analysis with different substrate lengths.

claim: The intrinsic translocation rate is ~40 amino acids per second for the proOmpA substrate.
source: After channel opening, translocation proceeds in two phases: a slow phase independent of substrate length, and a length-dependent transport phase with an intrinsic translocation rate of ~40 amino acids per second for the proOmpA substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the slope of the linear fit of dwell times versus substrate length shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Broad translocation rate distributions reflect the stochastic nature of polypeptide transport.
source: Broad translocation rate distributions reflect the stochastic nature of polypeptide transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broad distributions of dwell times observed in the experiments and is consistent with stochastic models.

claim: The major route for protein secretion is by way of the ubiquitous Sec machinery, comprising at its core a heterotrimeric complex: SecYEG in the plasma membrane of bacteria and archaea, and Sec61αβγ in the eukaryotic endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The major route for this process is by way of the ubiquitous Sec machinery, comprising at its core a heterotrimeric complex: SecYEG in the plasma membrane of bacteria and archaea, and Sec61αβγ in the eukaryotic endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Sec machinery across different domains of life.

claim: Pre-proteins are targeted to the Sec machinery with the aid of an N-terminal signal sequence (SS) or a trans-membrane helix (TMH).
source: Pre-proteins are targeted to the Sec machinery with the aid of an N-terminal signal sequence (SS) or a trans-membrane helix (TMH), and translocated through the Sec machinery in an unfolded conformation (Arkowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pre-proteins are translocated through the Sec machinery in an unfolded conformation.
source: Pre-proteins are targeted to the Sec machinery with the aid of an N-terminal signal sequence (SS) or a trans-membrane helix (TMH), and translocated through the Sec machinery in an unfolded conformation (Arkowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arkowitz et al., 1993.

claim: Protein translocation can occur either during synthesis (co-translationally), or afterwards (post-translationally).
source: This can occur either during their synthesis (co-translationally), or afterwards (post-translationally); in the latter case, pre-proteins are prevented from folding by cytosolic chaperones, such as SecB in bacteria (Kumamoto and Beckwith, 1983; Weiss et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing of protein translocation.

claim: In post-translational translocation, pre-proteins are prevented from folding by cytosolic chaperones, such as SecB in bacteria.
source: This can occur either during their synthesis (co-translationally), or afterwards (post-translationally); in the latter case, pre-proteins are prevented from folding by cytosolic chaperones, such as SecB in bacteria (Kumamoto and Beckwith, 1983; Weiss et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumamoto and Beckwith, 1983 and Weiss et al., 1988.

claim: Bacterial inner membrane proteins are generally secreted co-translationally.
source: Bacterial inner membrane proteins are generally secreted co-translationally, while proteins destined for the periplasm, outer membrane or the extra-cellular medium, tend to follow the post-translational route, driven there by the ATPase SecA (Hartl et al., 1990; Brundage et al., 1990; Lill et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteins destined for the periplasm, outer membrane or the extra-cellular medium tend to follow the post-translational route, driven by the ATPase SecA.
source: Bacterial inner membrane proteins are generally secreted co-translationally, while proteins destined for the periplasm, outer membrane or the extra-cellular medium, tend to follow the post-translational route, driven there by the ATPase SecA (Hartl et al., 1990; Brundage et al., 1990; Lill et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hartl et al., 1990; Brundage et al., 1990; Lill et al., 1989.

claim: The protein-channel is formed through the centre of SecY, between two pseudo-symmetrical halves, each containing five TMHs.
source: The protein-channel is formed through the centre of SecY, between two pseudo-symmetrical halves, each containing five TMHs (Figure 1) (Cannon et al., 2005; Van den Berg et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: When at rest the channel is kept closed by a short, usually α-helical plug and a ring of six hydrophobic residues.
source: When at rest the channel is kept closed by a short, usually α-helical plug and a ring of six hydrophobic residues, which serves to prevent ion leakage and dissipation of the proton motive force (PMF) (Figure 1A) (Saparov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saparov et al., 2007 and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The plug and ring of hydrophobic residues serve to prevent ion leakage and dissipation of the proton motive force (PMF).
source: When at rest the channel is kept closed by a short, usually α-helical plug and a ring of six hydrophobic residues, which serves to prevent ion leakage and dissipation of the proton motive force (PMF) (Figure 1A) (Saparov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saparov et al., 2007.

claim: Separation of the plug and hydrophobic ring opens a channel across the membrane (secretion) as well as a lateral gate (LG) for SS docking and membrane protein insertion.
source: Separation of these domains opens a channel across the membrane (secretion) as well as a lateral gate (LG) for SS docking and membrane protein insertion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on structural understanding and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Activation is achieved by the ribosome nascent chain complex.
source: Activation is achieved by the ribosome nascent chain complex (Jomaa et al., 2016; Voorhees and Hegde, 2016), or by association of pre-protein and SecA (Corey et al., 2016b; Lill et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jomaa et al., 2016 and Voorhees and Hegde, 2016.

claim: Activation is achieved by association of pre-protein and SecA.
source: Activation is achieved by the ribosome nascent chain complex (Jomaa et al., 2016; Voorhees and Hegde, 2016), or by association of pre-protein and SecA (Corey et al., 2016b; Lill et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Corey et al., 2016b and Lill et al., 1989.

claim: The bacterial initiation complex (pre-protein-SecA-SecYEG) undergoes a series of conformational changes prior to translocation.
source: Certainly, the bacterial initiation complex: pre-protein-SecA-SecYEG, undergoes a series of conformational changes prior to translocation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the initiation process.

claim: The initiation process involves the intercalation of the SS into the LG of SecY at the interface with the lipid bilayer, between TMH2 and TMH7.
source: This involves the intercalation of the SS into the LG of SecY – at the interface with the lipid bilayer, between TMHs 2 and 7 (Figure 1B) (Briggs et al., 1986; Hizlan et al., 2012; Li et al., 2016; McKnight et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple structural studies and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: SS intercalation causes TMH7 to relocate and the plug to become displaced from the channel, in a process termed 'unlocking'.
source: This in turn causes TMH7 to relocate and the plug to become displaced from the channel, in a process termed 'unlocking' (Corey et al., 2016b; Hizlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Corey et al., 2016b and Hizlan et al., 2012.

claim: The association of SecA causes a partial opening of the channel and the mobilisation of the pre-protein cross-linking domain of SecA, which forms a clamp around the translocating pre-protein.
source: Meanwhile, the association of SecA causes a partial opening of the channel and the mobilisation of the pre-protein cross-linking domain of SecA, which forms a clamp around the translocating pre-protein (Zimmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zimmer et al., 2008.

claim: The initiation steps lead to full activation of the SecA ATPase and prime the channel to translocate the remainder of the pre-protein.
source: Together, these steps lead to full activation of the SecA ATPase and prime the channel to translocate the remainder of the pre-protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described structural and biochemical changes.

claim: One proposed model for translocation is a processive power-stroke in which a fixed length of substrate is transported for each ATP molecule hydrolysed by SecA.
source: Two principal models have been proposed: (1) a processive power-stroke in which a fixed length of substrate is transported for each ATP molecule hydrolysed by SecA (Erlandson et al., 2008; Zimmer et al., 2008); and (2) a Brownian ratchet model whereby passive diffusive motion is conferred directionality by gating at the expense of ATP hydrolysis (Allen et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim describes a model proposed in the literature, supported by citations to Erlandson et al., 2008 and Zimmer et al., 2008.

claim: Another proposed model for translocation is a Brownian ratchet model whereby passive diffusive motion is conferred directionality by gating at the expense of ATP hydrolysis.
source: Two principal models have been proposed: (1) a processive power-stroke in which a fixed length of substrate is transported for each ATP molecule hydrolysed by SecA (Erlandson et al., 2008; Zimmer et al., 2008); and (2) a Brownian ratchet model whereby passive diffusive motion is conferred directionality by gating at the expense of ATP hydrolysis (Allen et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim describes a model proposed in the literature, supported by citations to Allen et al., 2016 and Liang et al., 2009a.

claim: Recent studies favour at least some element of diffusion in the translocation mechanism.
source: Recent studies favour at least some element of diffusion: previously, we proposed a 'pure' ratchet model, in which the free energy available from ATP binding and hydrolysis at SecA drives a Brownian ratchet at the SecY LG (Allen et al., 2016), while others have suggested a hybrid power stroke/diffusion model, in which ATP hydrolysis generates a power stroke ('push') on the polypeptide, followed by diffusion through the pore ('slide') (Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies including Allen et al., 2016 and Bauer et al., 2014.

claim: A 'pure' ratchet model has been proposed in which the free energy available from ATP binding and hydrolysis at SecA drives a Brownian ratchet at the SecY LG.
source: Recent studies favour at least some element of diffusion: previously, we proposed a 'pure' ratchet model, in which the free energy available from ATP binding and hydrolysis at SecA drives a Brownian ratchet at the SecY LG (Allen et al., 2016), while others have suggested a hybrid power stroke/diffusion model, in which ATP hydrolysis generates a power stroke ('push') on the polypeptide, followed by diffusion through the pore ('slide') (Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allen et al., 2016.

claim: A hybrid power stroke/diffusion model has been suggested in which ATP hydrolysis generates a power stroke ('push') on the polypeptide, followed by diffusion through the pore ('slide').
source: Recent studies favour at least some element of diffusion: previously, we proposed a 'pure' ratchet model, in which the free energy available from ATP binding and hydrolysis at SecA drives a Brownian ratchet at the SecY LG (Allen et al., 2016), while others have suggested a hybrid power stroke/diffusion model, in which ATP hydrolysis generates a power stroke ('push') on the polypeptide, followed by diffusion through the pore ('slide') (Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2014.

claim: There is a shift from purely power stroke models to a stochastic view which takes into account intrinsic dynamics of the complex.
source: This marks a shift from purely power stroke models based on static structural snapshots to a stochastic view in which intrinsic dynamics of the complex are taken into account (Corey et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Corey et al., 2016a.

claim: One study proposed a single ATP drives the passage of ~5 kDa of protein (roughly 40 amino acids) across the membrane.
source: This situation may explain why wildly different figures have been published for the energetic cost of transport: one study proposed a single ATP to drive the passage of ~5 kDa of protein (roughly 40 amino acids) across the membrane (van der Wolk et al., 1997), while a later analysis arrived at 5 molecules of ATP hydrolysed per single amino acid transported (Tomkiewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van der Wolk et al., 1997.

claim: A later analysis arrived at 5 molecules of ATP hydrolysed per single amino acid transported.
source: This situation may explain why wildly different figures have been published for the energetic cost of transport: one study proposed a single ATP to drive the passage of ~5 kDa of protein (roughly 40 amino acids) across the membrane (van der Wolk et al., 1997), while a later analysis arrived at 5 molecules of ATP hydrolysed per single amino acid transported (Tomkiewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tomkiewicz et al., 2006.

claim: Met63 (E. coli numbering) of the plug region of SecY was selected for dye attachment to monitor plug mobility.
source: Met63 (E. coli numbering) of the plug region of SecY was selected for dye attachment in order to monitor its mobility (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice made by the authors.

claim: Lys106 within the loop on the cytoplasmic side of SecY was chosen as the reference dye attachment site.
source: As FRET is most sensitive for inter-dye distances close to the Förster radius (6 nm for Alexa Fluor 488 and 594 dye pair used here), we chose the solvent-accessible residue Lys106, within the loop on the cytoplasmic side of SecY, as the reference dye attachment site (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice made by the authors.

claim: The Förster radius is 6 nm for Alexa Fluor 488 and 594 dye pair.
source: As FRET is most sensitive for inter-dye distances close to the Förster radius (6 nm for Alexa Fluor 488 and 594 dye pair used here), we chose the solvent-accessible residue Lys106, within the loop on the cytoplasmic side of SecY, as the reference dye attachment site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a known property of the dye pair used.

claim: Theoretical FRET efficiency histograms show low EFRET values (0.16–0.2) for the two open configurations.
source: The resulting inter-dye distance distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) yielded theoretical FRET efficiency (EFRET) histograms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) centred at low EFRET values (0.16–0.2) for the two open configurations sampled here and at 0.4 with ~0.6 shoulder for the closed state.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling of dye positions on crystal structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Theoretical FRET efficiency histograms show EFRET at 0.4 with ~0.6 shoulder for the closed state.
source: The resulting inter-dye distance distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) yielded theoretical FRET efficiency (EFRET) histograms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) centred at low EFRET values (0.16–0.2) for the two open configurations sampled here and at 0.4 with ~0.6 shoulder for the closed state.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling of dye positions on crystal structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The differences in FRET efficiency between open and closed states are sufficient to be distinguishable by single molecule FRET.
source: These differences are sufficient to be distinguishable by single molecule FRET; hence, M63 and K106 were mutated to cysteine in a Cys-free SecYEG variant (Deville et al., 2011), and the resulting protein was labelled with Alexa Fluor 488 and 594 maleimide dyes (the doubly labelled protein is hereafter designated SecYMKEG).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated FRET efficiency differences.

claim: The labelled SecYMKEG was fully active for transport.
source: Bulk transport assays utilising a model pre-protein substrate (233 amino acid long variant of proOmpA; see Materials and methods), showed that the labelled SecYMKEG was fully active for transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the transport assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Confocal microscopy allows detection of events on the millisecond timescale.
source: In order to capture the slow dwell times and potentially fast transitions, two complementary single molecule detection techniques were employed: confocal microscopy for detection of events on the millisecond timescale (Figure 2B) and total internal reflection (TIRF) imaging of immobilised vesicles for longer observations lasting up to several minutes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the confocal microscopy technique used.

claim: TIRF imaging of immobilised vesicles allows longer observations lasting up to several minutes.
source: In order to capture the slow dwell times and potentially fast transitions, two complementary single molecule detection techniques were employed: confocal microscopy for detection of events on the millisecond timescale (Figure 2B) and total internal reflection (TIRF) imaging of immobilised vesicles for longer observations lasting up to several minutes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the TIRF microscopy technique used.

claim: Confocal microscopy was used to explore the rate of interconversion between closed and open states.
source: The former allowed us to explore the rate of interconversion between closed and open states, whereas the latter was used to measure the duration of translocation and determine the translocation rate for individual SecYMKEG complexes.
evidence: This describes how the confocal microscopy data were used.

claim: TIRF microscopy was used to measure the duration of translocation and determine the translocation rate for individual SecYMKEG complexes.
source: The former allowed us to explore the rate of interconversion between closed and open states, whereas the latter was used to measure the duration of translocation and determine the translocation rate for individual SecYMKEG complexes.
evidence: This describes how the TIRF microscopy data were used.

claim: Both confocal and TIRF methods yield histograms that show co-existence of two states with EFRET ~0.2 and ~0.4–0.6.
source: Both methods thus yield histograms that show co-existence of two states with EFRET ~0.2 and~0.4–0.6, which in turn are comparable to the values predicted for the respective open and closed states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: The observed EFRET values are comparable to the values predicted for the respective open and closed states.
source: Both methods thus yield histograms that show co-existence of two states with EFRET ~0.2 and~0.4–0.6, which in turn are comparable to the values predicted for the respective open and closed states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim compares experimental data with theoretical predictions.

claim: The similarity of the histograms obtained by the two methods suggests no bias in the representation of each state under steady-state conditions.
source: The similarity of the histograms obtained by the two methods also suggests no bias in the representation of each state under steady-state conditions, irrespective of whether SecYMKEG is immobilised to a surface or placed into a freely diffusing proteoliposome in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of results from two different methods.

claim: The approximately equal populations of the open and closed states are a result of the steady state conditions in which complexes spend roughly an equal time unoccupied (closed) or engaged in translocation (open).
source: The approximately equal populations of the open and closed states are a result of the steady state conditions in which complexes spend roughly an equal time unoccupied, waiting for the next initiation event (closed), or are engaged in translocation (open).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed equal populations under steady-state conditions.

claim: The same complex undergoes multiple turnovers in the absence of signal peptidase.
source: As seen in the example TIRF trace in Figure 2F, the same complex undergoes multiple turnovers; yet, the experiments were performed in the absence of signal peptidase, required in vivo to liberate the secreted polypeptide from the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TIRF trace shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The SS must be able to diffuse spontaneously away from the translocon and into the membrane.
source: Therefore, the SS must be able to diffuse spontaneously away from the translocon and into the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of multiple turnovers without signal peptidase.

claim: Pre-protein maturation occurs late or post-translocation.
source: This is compatible with pre-protein maturation occurring late or post-translocation (Josefsson and Randall, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Josefsson and Randall, 1981 and is consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: SecYMKEG alone shows a peak in the FRET histogram at EFRET ~ 0.35.
source: Surprisingly, a peak was found in the FRET histogram at EFRET ~ 0.35 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A); that is lower than expected for the closed state observed in the structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SecYMKEG with saturating SecA and ATP, but without proOmpA, reproduces the low FRET closed state.
source: Hence, another control, containing SecYMKEG, saturating SecA and ATP, but without proOmpA, was examined and indeed the FRET efficiency histogram reproduces that of the low FRET closed state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fully closed state is only attained within the SecYMKEG:SecA complex.
source: This suggests that the fully closed state is only attained within the SecYMKEG:SecA complex, while SecYMKEG alone is either undergoing dynamic rapid exchange between open and closed states, and/or samples partially open states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of FRET histograms for SecYMKEG alone versus SecYMKEG:SecA.

claim: Addition of excess AMP-PNP to a translocation reaction results in a FRET distribution with a peak below 0.2, representing a trapped open state.
source: The open state control was prepared by first saturating SecYMKEG proteoliposomes with proOmpA and SecA in the presence of saturating ATP (1 mM), then rapidly quenching the translocation reaction by addition of excess AMP-PNP (5 mM) – a non-hydrolysable analogue of ATP, previously shown to keep the translocation complex intact (Deville et al., 2011). This condition resulted in a FRET distribution with a peak below 0.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), as expected for a trapped open state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to Deville et al., 2011.

claim: The attached dyes have not drastically perturbed the properties of the channel.
source: This suggests the attached dyes have not drastically perturbed the properties of the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that FRET distributions are predictably affected by SecYEG variants.

claim: The opening time constant increases with decreasing ATP concentration.
source: Figure 3D shows the opening time constant in the presence of SecA, SecB and proOmpA increases with decreasing ATP concentration, while closing happens on a ~ 10 ms timescale and does not depend on ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Closing happens on a ~ 10 ms timescale and does not depend on ATP.
source: Figure 3D shows the opening time constant in the presence of SecA, SecB and proOmpA increases with decreasing ATP concentration, while closing happens on a ~ 10 ms timescale and does not depend on ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The opening time constant converges to 10 ms at saturating ATP concentration.
source: The opening time constant also converges to 10 ms in a saturating ATP concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The apparent concentration at which the opening process is at its half maximum rate (K50%) is ~ 56 μM.
source: The apparent concentration at which the opening process is at its half maximum rate, K50% ~ 56 μM, obtained by fitting these data, is similar to that of the SecA ATPase KM ~50 μM (Robson et al., 2009a), suggesting that ATP hydrolysis is required for the initial plug opening.
evidence: This claim is based on fitting the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The K50% for opening is similar to the SecA ATPase KM of ~50 μM.
source: The apparent concentration at which the opening process is at its half maximum rate, K50% ~ 56 μM, obtained by fitting these data, is similar to that of the SecA ATPase KM ~50 μM (Robson et al., 2009a), suggesting that ATP hydrolysis is required for the initial plug opening.
evidence: This claim compares the measured K50% with the known KM of SecA ATPase from Robson et al., 2009a.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required for the initial plug opening.
source: The apparent concentration at which the opening process is at its half maximum rate, K50% ~ 56 μM, obtained by fitting these data, is similar to that of the SecA ATPase KM ~50 μM (Robson et al., 2009a), suggesting that ATP hydrolysis is required for the initial plug opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between K50% for opening and the KM of SecA ATPase.

claim: In the absence of proOmpA there are only rare spontaneous opening and closing events, with time constants that do not depend on ATP concentration.
source: In the absence of proOmpA there are only rare spontaneous opening and closing events, with time constants that do not depend on ATP concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the presence of SecA, proOmpA and AMP-PNP, SecYMKEG remains in the closed state.
source: In the presence of SecA, proOmpA and AMP-PNP, SecYMKEG remains in the closed state (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis together with pre-protein substrate engagement are needed to fully displace the plug from the channel.
source: Therefore, ATP binding and hydrolysis together with pre-protein substrate engagement are needed to fully displace the plug from the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations with ATP, AMP-PNP, and proOmpA.

claim: The activation energy for opening is Ea ~61 kJ/mol.
source: The activation energy for opening, Ea ~61 kJ/mol, is close to the value measured for SecA ATPase activity in the presence of translocating substrate or signal peptide (66 kJ/mol), but much lower than that of SecYMKEG:SecA alone (~180 kJ/mol) (Gouridis et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on the Arrhenius plot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The activation energy for opening is close to the value measured for SecA ATPase activity in the presence of translocating substrate or signal peptide (66 kJ/mol).
source: The activation energy for opening, Ea ~61 kJ/mol, is close to the value measured for SecA ATPase activity in the presence of translocating substrate or signal peptide (66 kJ/mol), but much lower than that of SecYMKEG:SecA alone (~180 kJ/mol) (Gouridis et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim compares the measured activation energy with values from Gouridis et al., 2009.

claim: The activation energy for opening is much lower than that of SecYMKEG:SecA alone (~180 kJ/mol).
source: The activation energy for opening, Ea ~61 kJ/mol, is close to the value measured for SecA ATPase activity in the presence of translocating substrate or signal peptide (66 kJ/mol), but much lower than that of SecYMKEG:SecA alone (~180 kJ/mol) (Gouridis et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim compares the measured activation energy with values from Gouridis et al., 2009.

claim: The ATP-driven plug opening is performed by SecA in complex with SecYMKEG pre-activated by the SS.
source: This suggests that the ATP-driven plug opening is performed by SecA in complex with SecYMKEG pre-activated by the SS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the activation energy measurements.

claim: The plug closing exhibits activation energy of Ea ~45 kJ/mol.
source: Furthermore, the plug closing exhibits significantly lower activation energy – Ea ~45 kJ/mol, which is below values reported for ATPases (60–70 kJ/mol) (Jenkins et al., 1999), consistent with the results shown in Figure 3D that closing is independent of ATP.
evidence: This claim is based on the Arrhenius plot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The activation energy for plug closing is below values reported for ATPases (60–70 kJ/mol).
source: Furthermore, the plug closing exhibits significantly lower activation energy – Ea ~45 kJ/mol, which is below values reported for ATPases (60–70 kJ/mol) (Jenkins et al., 1999), consistent with the results shown in Figure 3D that closing is independent of ATP.
evidence: This claim compares the measured activation energy with values from Jenkins et al., 1999.

claim: The low activation energy for plug closing is consistent with closing being independent of ATP.
source: Furthermore, the plug closing exhibits significantly lower activation energy – Ea ~45 kJ/mol, which is below values reported for ATPases (60–70 kJ/mol) (Jenkins et al., 1999), consistent with the results shown in Figure 3D that closing is independent of ATP.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the activation energy measurement with the ATP independence of closing.

claim: SecYMKEG alone shows considerable static heterogeneity and dynamics.
source: SecYMKEG alone shows considerable static heterogeneity (spread along the diagonal) and dynamics (off-diagonal spots), with a broad diffuse spot between the closed and open configurations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The open state of SecYMKEG alone is only transiently populated and returns to a partly open configuration.
source: However, judging from the absence of density at the stationary position of the open state (E1 = 0.2, E2 = 0.2 area in Figure 4A, area marked with *) the open state is only transiently populated and returns to a partly open configuration (E1 = 0.2, E2 = 0.3 density region in Figure 4A, area marked with #).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The transient nature of conformational diversions in SecYMKEG alone is demonstrated by only a small contribution of the open state to the equilibrium histogram (<7%).
source: The transient nature of these conformational diversions is further demonstrated by only a small contribution of the open state to the equilibrium histogram in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (<7%) and is consistent with low ion conductivity of SecYEG (Saparov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the equilibrium histogram data and citation to Saparov et al., 2007.

claim: The plug populates predominantly the expected closed state (EFRET ~0.4) in the plug stabilising mutant SecYR357E.
source: By contrast, the plug populates predominantly the expected closed state (EFRET ~0.4) in a plug stabilising mutant SecYR357E (the labelled mutant designated SecYMK,R357EEG) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Tam et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Tam et al., 2005.

claim: The plug can be localised in the open state by disulfide bond cross-linking with SecE.
source: This finding is consistent with previous reports showing the plug can be localised in the open state by disulfide bond cross-linking with SecE (Harris and Silhavy, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris and Silhavy, 1999.

claim: Cross-links between the plug and SecE are reduced when the R357E mutant is incorporated, due to its tendency to retain the plug in the central closed position.
source: These cross-links are reduced when the R357E mutant is incorporated, due to its tendency to retain the plug in the central closed position (Tam et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tam et al., 2005.

claim: Addition of SecA to SecYMKEG results in the formation of a more stable complex, with the plug predominantly residing in the high-FRET (closed) state.
source: Addition of SecA to SecYMKEG results in the formation of a more stable complex, with the plug predominantly residing in the high-FRET (closed) state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The active translocon (SecYMKEG:SecA with proOmpA, SecB and saturating ATP) shows the plug shifts into a predominantly open state at steady-state.
source: The active translocon was assembled by addition of proOmpA (100 aa long variant), SecB and saturating ATP to SecYMKEG:SecA. The RASP analysis at steady-state (>5 min) shows, as expected, that the plug shifts into a predominantly open state, with some minor closing transitions represented by a smear to higher FRET along the E1 axis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The active complex at sub-saturating ATP concentration (0.1 mM) is much more dynamic than at saturating ATP.
source: This behaviour is distinct from the same active complex at sub-saturating ATP concentration (0.1 mM), which is much more dynamic (Figure 4D): under these conditions, the FRET landscape is characterised by a significant population of the closed states transitioning to the open state (Figure 4D, off-diagonal smear along E2 axis).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Plug opening is dependent on ATP.
source: This confirms that plug opening is indeed dependent on ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of behavior at saturating versus sub-saturating ATP concentrations.

claim: The SS can unlock the translocon in trans and initiate the translocation of mature substrates lacking a SS.
source: It has been shown previously that the SS can unlock the translocon in trans and initiate the translocation of mature substrates, that is those lacking a SS (Gouridis et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gouridis et al., 2009.

claim: SS association displaces the plug from the central location in SecY.
source: Furthermore, this association has also shown to displace the plug from the central location in SecY (Hizlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hizlan et al., 2012.

claim: Addition of OmpA and SS to SecYMKEG:SecA in the presence of saturating ATP results in plug opening similar to that observed for addition of proOmpA.
source: The addition of OmpA and SS resulted in plug opening (Figure 4E) akin to that observed for addition of proOmpA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figures 4E and 4C.

claim: The SS can act in trans to promote plug opening.
source: Therefore, the SS can indeed act in trans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that OmpA plus SS in trans produces similar opening as proOmpA.

claim: OmpA alone does not bring about plug opening.
source: As expected OmpA alone did not bring about plug opening (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When the SS is added to SecYMKEG:SecA in the absence of OmpA, with either ATP or AMPPNP, or even with SecA also absent, the plug assumes a new state with EFRET ~ 0.25.
source: Interestingly, when the SS was added to SecYMKEG:SecA in the absence of OmpA, with either ATP or AMPPNP (Figure 4G,H), or even with SecA also absent (Figure 4I) – the plug assumes a new aparently static state with EFRET ~ 0.25: note diagonal localisation within the E1-E2 transition density plot (Figure 4G–I)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figures 4G, 4H, and 4I.

claim: The EFRET ~ 0.25 state is static on the sub-millisecond timescale.
source: BVA of the SecYMKEG:SecA:SS complex and SecYMKEG:SS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D, respectively) clearly remain static on the sub-millisecond timescale (compare with Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Burst Variance Analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The EFRET ~ 0.25 is a genuine, part open state representing the 'unlocked' configuration of the translocon.
source: Thus, we conclude that the EFRET ~ 0.25 is indeed a genuine, part open state. Such assignment is consistent with the previous observation of increased plug crosslinking to SecE upon prolonged incubation with a pre-protein, which was interpreted as partial opening of the plug (Tam et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the BVA analysis and is consistent with previous observations cited from Tam et al., 2005.

claim: Binding of the SS is sufficient to unlock the complex (EFRET ~0.25).
source: The results presented here also confirm that binding of the SS is sufficient to unlock the complex (EFRET ~0.25), while full opening (EFRET ~0.2) is only achieved in the presence of complete protein substrate and ATP hydrolysis by SecA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations with SS alone versus SS plus substrate and ATP.

claim: Full opening (EFRET ~0.2) is only achieved in the presence of complete protein substrate and ATP hydrolysis by SecA.
source: The results presented here also confirm that binding of the SS is sufficient to unlock the complex (EFRET ~0.25), while full opening (EFRET ~0.2) is only achieved in the presence of complete protein substrate and ATP hydrolysis by SecA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations comparing different conditions.

claim: In the presence of non-hydrolysable AMP-PNP, SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB:proOmpA remains fully closed.
source: Indeed, in the presence of non-hydrolysable AMP-PNP SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB:proOmpA remains fully closed (Figure 4J), as is the case when the SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB complex is presented with a defective SS, wherein four critical residues of the hydrophobic core were deleted proOmpA∆IAIA7-10 (Emr et al., 1980) (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4J and citation to Emr et al., 1980.

claim: When presented with a defective SS (proOmpA∆IAIA7-10), the SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB complex remains fully closed.
source: Indeed, in the presence of non-hydrolysable AMP-PNP SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB:proOmpA remains fully closed (Figure 4J), as is the case when the SecYMKEG:SecA:SecB complex is presented with a defective SS, wherein four critical residues of the hydrophobic core were deleted proOmpA∆IAIA7-10 (Emr et al., 1980) (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RASP analysis shown in Figure 4K and citation to Emr et al., 1980.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required for SecYEG to achieve a fully open channel and for initial intercalation of the mature region of the pre-protein.
source: The confirmation that the SS is alone is critical for the unlocked complex suggests that ATP hydrolysis is required for SecYEG to achieve a fully open channel and for initial intercalation of the mature region of the pre-protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations with AMP-PNP and defective SS.

claim: The plug stabilising mutant (SecYMK,R357EEG) fails to open in conditions that would normally promote translocation.
source: As expected, the plug stabilising mutant (SecYMK,R357EEG) fails to open in conditions that would normally promote translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations with the R357E mutant.

claim: The R357E mutation does not disrupt SecA binding.
source: The presence of SecA eliminates the part open ensemble (compare Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) in a fashion similar to the wt SecYMKEG:SecA (Figure 4B and J), indicating that this mutation, while located on the cytoplasmic side close to the SecA binding site, does not disrupt SecA binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of behavior of the mutant with wild-type in the presence of SecA.

claim: The R357E substitution likely disrupts an allosteric path within SecYEG that is involved in coupling the ATPase cycle of SecA to plug opening.
source: Thus, the R357E substitution likely disrupts an allosteric path within SecYEG that is involved in the coupling ATPase cycle of SecA to the plug opening.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects of the R357E mutation.

claim: All proOmpA substrates of various lengths (100 to 683 aa) were transported successfully into proteoliposomes.
source: All these substrates were transported successfully into proteoliposomes as shown by ensemble translocation assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and by the stimulation of the ATPase activity of SecA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ensemble translocation assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and ATPase assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: All proOmpA substrates stimulated the ATPase activity of SecA.
source: All these substrates were transported successfully into proteoliposomes as shown by ensemble translocation assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and by the stimulation of the ATPase activity of SecA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATPase assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dwell times of the open state clearly increase with the length of the substrate.
source: However, the dwell times of the open state clearly increases with the length of the substrate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The closed state dwell time shows no dependence on the length of polypeptide chain.
source: By contrast, a similar analysis for the closed state (EFRET ~0.4) shows no dependence of the dwell time on the length of polypeptide chain (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The closed state dwell time represents an average wait prior to, or between, translocation events and reflects the rate of assembly of the active complexes.
source: This is not surprising: the closed state dwell time represents an average wait prior to, or between, translocation events and thus reflects the rate of assembly of the active complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the closed state dwell time data.

claim: The dwell time of the open state increases at sub-saturating ATP concentrations.
source: If the dwell time of the open state is indeed measuring translocation time, then it should increase at sub-saturating ATP concentrations. As shown in Figure 5B, this is indeed the case, and the dependence is consistent with a steady state KM ~ 50 μM as measured previously for the SecA ATPase (Robson et al., 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ATP dependence of open state dwell time is consistent with a steady state KM ~ 50 μM as measured previously for the SecA ATPase.
source: If the dwell time of the open state is indeed measuring translocation time, then it should increase at sub-saturating ATP concentrations. As shown in Figure 5B, this is indeed the case, and the dependence is consistent with a steady state KM ~ 50 μM as measured previously for the SecA ATPase (Robson et al., 2009b).
evidence: This claim compares the experimental data with the known KM from Robson et al., 2009b.

claim: The translocation rate is ~40 ± 6 aa/s and is independent of the cytoplasmic chaperone SecB.
source: The resulting rate is ~40 ± 6 aa/s and within statistical error is independent of the cytoplasmic chaperone SecB (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on the linear fit of dwell times versus substrate length shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a significant fixed, length-independent dwell time component of ~5 s in the absence of SecB.
source: An extrapolation of the least squares fit line to zero substrate length suggests that there is a significant fixed, length-independent dwell time component of ~5 s in the absence of SecB (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on the intercept of the linear fit shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The slow phase is related to the delivery of the substrate to SecA, with SecB making the initial handover and delivery of substrate more efficient.
source: As SecB acts on the cytoplasmic side, this suggests this slow phase is related to the delivery of the substrate to SecA – with SecB presumably making the initial handover and delivery of substrate more efficient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of SecB on the constant dwell time component.

claim: SecB reduces ATP consumption as indicated by ensemble ATPase assays with SecA.
source: This is consistent with the observation that SecB reduces ATP consumption, as indicated by ensemble ATPase assays with SecA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The plug closure time is less than 10 ms.
source: Given the plug closure time is less than 10 ms (Figure 3D) and SecYMKEG complex alone seldom visits the open state in equilibrium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) the retention of the open state after the completion of the translocation is unlikely.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The constant dwell time is assigned to a slow initial translocation phase, which follows ATP-driven opening of the plug and is accelerated by SecB.
source: Hence, we assign the constant dwell time to a slow initial translocation phase, which follows ATP-driven opening of the plug and is accelerated by SecB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of dwell times and the effect of SecB.

claim: The rate of processive translocation is higher than the previously reported value of ~30 aa/s.
source: The rate of processive translocation is higher than the previously reported value of ~30 aa/s which were also estimated using proOmpA substrates with various chain lengths, but in the absence of SecB (De Keyzer et al., 2002; Tomkiewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim compares the measured rate with previously reported values from De Keyzer et al., 2002 and Tomkiewicz et al., 2006.

claim: The difference in translocation rate compared to previous studies is explained by the slow translocation phase, which is substantial only in the absence of SecB.
source: The difference is readily explained by the slow translocation phase, which is substantial only in the absence of SecB.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the discrepancy with previous studies.

claim: In the presence of SecB, the rate would support transport of typical individual precursors (100 to 1000 amino acids) within 25 s.
source: In the presence of SecB, the rate estimated here would support transport of typical individual precursors (100 to 1000 amino acids) within 25 s which is close to the previously estimated transport requirements (~20 s per substrate) in rapidly dividing E. coli cells (Brundage et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured translocation rate and comparison with requirements from Brundage et al., 1990.

claim: Channel closure is fast (<10 ms) and ATP independent.
source: Channel closure monitored by the relocation of the plug is fast (<10 ms) and ATP independent.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Channel closure does not impose any limitation on the overall translocation efficiency.
source: Hence, it does not seem to impose any limitation on the overall translocation efficiency (state (7) to (8) in Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fast closure time.

claim: A single translocon is capable of multiple rounds of translocation for proOmpA, even in the absence of signal peptidase.
source: Evidently, a single translocon is capable of multiple rounds of translocation, at least for proOmpA, even in the absence of signal peptidase.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of multiple turnovers in TIRF traces.

claim: The signal peptide together with the rest of the substrate is able to diffuse from the translocon and does not perturb plug closure.
source: This suggests that the signal peptide together with the rest of the substrate is able to diffuse from the translocon and does not perturb plug closure (state (8) to (1) in Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of multiple turnovers without signal peptidase.
